name: Hazel
lede: Hazel is named for the hazelnut and the shrub it grows on; Paterson files it among the browns, while this screen swatch is a darker, greener gold.

sections.title: The nut behind the name
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary gives two old words for the same nut. *Avellaneous* is the light brown of the hazelnut or filbert, and *nut-brown* is often the reddish brown of the hazelnut, though strictly it covers all nut colors [1][2]. The English name hazel is listed in Paterson's index among the browns [3].

Maerz and Paul record hazel as a color name from 1592, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files this swatch in its block 57 [4]. On a screen, the swatch is a dark olive-gold, with more green in it than the nut has [4]. In the Werner and Syme tradition, hazel nuts appear among the example objects in the reds and browns [5].

sections.title: A tree with a reputation
sections.body:
Before it was a color, hazel was a tree with meanings. In the medieval tree symbolism Pastoureau describes, the hazel and the hornbeam were linked with magic, and the hazel was one of a few trees thought ambivalent, together with the poplar and the cypress [6]. Fairies, who were associated with green, were said to guard the plants they drew power from, among them hawthorn, service tree and hazel [7]. The color carries none of this meaning; the name does.

Hazel also served as an observation word. A medical color table of the early nineteenth century that borrowed Syme's names lists hazel and [[chestnut|lighter chestnut]] among the browns, beside wood brown and [[tawny]] orange [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Hazel is a middling-common color in our painting archive: 339 of 23,781 paintings, 1.43 per cent, and more common than 72 per cent of the named colors [8]. The within-painting count is 217 paintings, in which it most often plays an accent, as it does in 60 per cent of them [8]. It peaks in the 1800s, in 1.2 per cent of the 8,345 paintings from then, 1.3 times the museums' baseline [8].

The painters who use it most are [[painter:paulus-potter|Paulus Potter]], in 7 of the 28 works we have, 9.4 times the baseline, and [[painter:luis-egidio-melendez|Luis Egidio Meléndez]], in 6 of 39 [8]. India is the most over-represented country, with 12 of 721 paintings [8]. Our earliest match is a work of 1330 by Pietro Lorenzetti, a floor set by a thin early archive, not a first [8].

As ever, these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue and not a pigment test, and this swatch is darker and greener than the hazelnut brown a reader might expect [8]. The word itself, counted as a color adjective in Google Books, peaks in the 2010s [8].
